paras: The Cochran cabin shooting was a night attack by a disguised party of young white men on the cabin of John Brown, a Black man living near Cochran, Georgia, in August 1880, in which Brown killed two of the attackers, brothers named Dykes, with a shotgun. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. Northern papers reported it as a Black man's defense of his home and remarked on the Southern jury's verdict.

According to a special dispatch from Cincinnati to the Chicago Tribune, Brown was 'a peaceable negro citizen' who had recently had 'a difficulty about work' with two young farmers, Frank and Mack Dykes. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union, in an editorial, offered a different motive, calling the attackers 'bulldozers' who meant to punish a Black man 'who had dared to think for himself in politics', though it named no source for this.

The attack came on the night of Wednesday, August 25, according to the Atlanta dispatch, and at midnight according to the Cincinnati one. In the Atlanta version, four young white men in disguise went to Brown's cabin, broke down the door and began firing into it. The Cincinnati dispatch instead described two armed, disguised men who demanded entrance to whip Brown and, when he refused to open the door, fired at him twice.

Brown seized a double-barreled gun loaded with buckshot and fired both barrels, killing two brothers named Dykes; the wire added that 'the tops of their heads were blown off'. He recognized the dead men as Frank and Mack Dykes, according to the Cincinnati dispatch and an Ohio weekly that condensed it.

The Atlanta wire said that Brown 'made his escape', while the Cincinnati dispatch said he notified the authorities. A coroner's jury, sitting before 'a great crowd' in the Cincinnati account, returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, finding that Brown had acted in self-defense. The same dispatch reported that a good part of the public endorsed Brown's course and that many citizens promised him any help he might need. No report of arrests of any surviving attackers, or of other legal action, appears in the coverage.

The Atlanta dispatch of August 27 appeared that day in the Washington Evening Star under the headline 'The Killers Killed', and in the Rock Island Argus and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer. On August 28 it ran in the New-York Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, often under the heading 'Justifiable Homicide'. The same day it appeared in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette, the Dallas Daily Herald and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer. Weeklies in South Carolina, Vermont and Minnesota carried condensed versions into early September.

Many headlines took Brown's side: the New-York Tribune used 'A Negro Defends His Home', the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer 'A Most Righteous Verdict', and the Weekly Arizona Citizen 'Served Him Right'. A Wilmington, Delaware, paper headed the wire 'Bloods Get Their Dues' and, on another page, called the attackers 'four young white ruffians', while the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer called them 'a Gang of Outlaws'. The Dallas Daily Herald headed its copy 'Two Brothers Killed while Attempting to Mob a Negro'.

The Chicago Tribune's own dispatch, headed 'Ku-Kluxed the Wrong Negro', called the affair 'a case of Ku-Kluxing with a happy termination' and said many citizens approved Brown's 'pluck'. On August 30 the Sacramento Daily Record-Union drew a campaign lesson in an editorial, writing that 'if there had been more negroes like this one bulldozing would have gone out of fashion long ago' and calling the jury's verdict 'by far the most remarkable fact in the case'. In Georgia, the only paper found to carry the story, the Marietta Journal, reprinted the wire word for word among its 'Georgia Gleanings' on September 2, without comment or local detail.

Accounts differed on the number of attackers: the Atlanta wire said four young white men came to the cabin, while the Cincinnati dispatch and the Somerset Press of Ohio described two, both of whom were killed. Most versions dated the attack to Wednesday night, but the Green-Mountain Freeman of Montpelier, Vermont, condensing the wire, gave it as Tuesday night. The motive appeared as a dispute over work in the Cincinnati dispatch and as politics in the Sacramento editorial, while the Atlanta wire gave none.

reader.title: Cochran cabin shooting
bases: A disguised party of young white men came to a Black man's cabin at night, by one account to whip him, and fired into it; the Chicago Tribune's dispatch called it 'Ku-Kluxing' (A1, A4).

The intended victim, John Brown, survived and killed two of the attackers; the only deaths were of the attackers, so no one was killed by the group (A1, A4). The group was four by the Atlanta wire and two by the Cincinnati dispatch (A1, A4).

Two independent dispatches, the Atlanta wire and a Cincinnati special to the Chicago Tribune, agree that Brown shot and killed two Dykes brothers who attacked his cabin at night and that a coroner's jury cleared him, though they differ on the number of attackers (A1, A4).

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Four disguised young white men broke down the door of Brown's cabin on Wednesday night and fired into it; Brown killed two Dykes brothers with buckshot and escaped; the coroner's jury found justifiable homicide.

accounts.label: Cincinnati special dispatch
accounts.gist: Two armed, disguised men demanded entrance at midnight to whip Brown and fired at him twice; he killed both, recognized them as Frank and Mack Dykes, with whom he had a work dispute, notified the authorities, and was cleared by an inquest that found self-defense.

accounts.label: Sacramento editorial
accounts.gist: A party of bulldozers came to outrage a Black man 'who had dared to think for himself in politics' and he killed two; the verdict showed Southern Democrats bending to campaign needs.

framing.detail: The Atlanta wire ran without comment in dozens of papers, often under 'Justifiable Homicide'.
Headlines condemned the attackers: 'A Negro Defends His Home', 'A Most Righteous Verdict', 'Served Him Right', 'Bloods Get Their Dues', 'a Gang of Outlaws'.
The Chicago Tribune's dispatch, 'Ku-Kluxed the Wrong Negro', called it Ku-Kluxing 'with a happy termination' and praised Brown's 'pluck'.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union editorial praised Brown's resistance to bulldozing and read the verdict in terms of the presidential campaign.
The one Georgia paper found, the Marietta Journal, reprinted the wire among 'Georgia Gleanings' without comment.
